messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rajesh first felt the weight of what he had done on a gray morning off the coast of Alaska, thirty years ago. He was a petty officer on a Coast Guard cutter, and during a rough-weather rescue, a line he had secured snapped under tension. The metal hook whipped back and struck a younger crewman in the temple. The man went overboard before anyone could grab him, and by the time they pulled him from the water, he was gone. Rajesh had been the one to secure that line. He had checked it twice, but in the chaos, he had missed a fray. In the weeks that followed, the official inquiry cleared him—mechanical failure, they said—but Rajesh could not shake the image of the man’s face, the way his eyes had gone wide a second before the hook flew. He told himself it was an accident, that he was not to blame, but the thought never fully settled.

Now, at eighty, widowed and living alone in a quiet coastal town, Rajesh found that the past was no longer content to stay buried. It surfaced in pieces—disconnected fragments that made no sense together. He might be standing at the kitchen sink, washing a dish, and suddenly he would feel the cold spray of the Bering Sea on his face, smell the diesel and salt, hear the frantic radio chatter. The memory came back fully, across every sense, and for a moment he was there again, his hands numb, his heart hammering. But when he tried to deliberately recall what happened—when he sat down to make sense of it—the details scattered. He could not hold the sequence in his mind. He knew only the feeling: a sickening lurch in his gut, and the conviction that he was fundamentally broken.

The triggers were everywhere, though he had not always recognized them. A walk along the beach, with the wind off the water and the sound of waves, would seize him without warning. The sight of a rope or a coil of cable in a hardware store would make his chest tighten. Sirens—ambulances, fire trucks—sent him into a cold sweat, because they reminded him of the rescue helicopter that had arrived too late. And conversations about the future, even casual ones with his daughter about her children’s college plans, made him feel as though he had no right to look ahead. He had come to believe that the event happened because of the sort of person he was—careless, unworthy, dangerous. He was certain that he had to be on guard all the time, because the world was full of moments that could crack him open.

These beliefs shaped how he lived. He avoided unfamiliar places entirely, sticking to the same two-mile radius he had walked for years. In the grocery store, he always chose a seat at the back of the café, with his back to the wall and a clear view of the door. He found himself taking small, unnecessary risks—driving a little too fast on empty roads, leaving the stove on for a few minutes after cooking—as if punishing himself for what he had done. When the memories came, he tried to push them out of his mind. He would force himself to think only positive thoughts: his grandchildren’s laughter, a good meal, the sun on the water. Sometimes he told himself the event did not really happen, or that it was not that bad. But the harder he pushed, the more the fragments returned, and the more convinced he became that he was defective.

The cycles tightened over the months. A siren would wail in the distance, and Rajesh would feel his throat close. That sound would drag him into a fragmented reliving—the helicopter rotors, the shouting, the cold—and from that reliving, the belief that he was a bad person would surge up, raw and undeniable. To escape it, he would force himself to think of something else, anything else, but the effort only made the next trigger more potent. He began scanning every environment for threats: the angle of a shadow, the sound of footsteps behind him, the way a stranger glanced his way. He was certain that if he let his guard down, the memory would drown him.

His daughter noticed that he had stopped coming to family dinners. She called more often, but he let the phone ring. He could not explain why. The only thing that brought him to the clinic, finally, was a conversation with his doctor during a routine checkup. The doctor asked about his mood, and Rajesh, for the first time, said that he did not feel safe in his own mind. He was most afraid that if he let himself remember fully, he would finally see the truth: that he was the sort of person who kills other people. But he was also tired—tired of the vigilance, the rituals, the way his life had shrunk to a few safe streets and a chair with a clear view of the door. He wanted to know if it was possible to live differently, even at his age.
